title: The Straight Sceptre
note: The justice a ruler gives. It leans to neither side, like a straight rod, so it is called the sceptre. Only a ruler free of lapses can give it.

couplets.plain: To look into it, show no favour to anyone, hold to fairness and act after weighing it: that is justice.
couplets.pm: When those under him do wrong, a ruler looks into the offence, shows no favour to anyone, even those dearer than life, and holds to the fairness that is a ruler’s nature. He weighs with the learned the punishment set for that offence and gives exactly that much. This is justice.

links.quote: that is justice

couplets.plain: All the world lives looking to the sky. A ruler’s people live looking to his sceptre.
couplets.pm: All living things in the world depend on rain, and subjects depend on the ruler’s straight sceptre. The sky stands for the food it brings, and the sceptre for the safety it brings. Without that safety, even food is no use to the people.

links.quote: A ruler’s people live looking to his sceptre
A ruler’s people
All the world lives looking to the sky
links.reason: The sky everyone looks to for rain stands for a ruler everyone depends on.

links.quote: looking to his sceptre

couplets.plain: The ruler’s sceptre stands at the root of the books of the sages and of righteousness.
couplets.pm: The ruler’s straight sceptre stands as the cause of the Vedas of the sages and of the righteousness they teach. The Vedas belong to rulers and merchants too, but they are named for the sages as the foremost. The Vedas and righteousness have no beginning, yet they can’t go on without the sceptre, so it is called their source. Nothing is the source of it.

links.quote: at the root of the books of the sages and of righteousness
the books of the sages
links.reason: Places the books of the sages under the ruler’s protection.

links.quote: The ruler’s sceptre stands

couplets.plain: The world clings to the feet of the great ruler who holds his people close and wields the sceptre.
couplets.pm: People won’t let go of the feet of the ruler of the great earth who embraces his subjects and wields the straight sceptre. Embracing means speaking sweetly and giving what they need when they are weak. One who does both without fail rules the whole earth, and all have a loving-kindness for him that never leaves.

links.quote: holds his people close and wields the sceptre
links.reason: Caring rule is repaid by a world that clings to the ruler’s feet.

links.quote: the great ruler

couplets.plain: Rain and harvest come together in the land of a ruler who wields the sceptre as it should be wielded.
couplets.pm: Rain in season and undiminished harvests come together in the land of a ruler who wields the straight sceptre in the way the books lay down. Sky and earth work as one and plenty flows.

links.quote: Rain and harvest come together
a ruler who wields the sceptre as it should be wielded
wields the sceptre as it should be wielded

couplets.plain: It is not the spear that brings a ruler victory. It is the sceptre, and that only if it doesn’t bend.
couplets.pm: What gives a ruler victory in battle is not the spear he throws but the sceptre, and that only if it doesn’t lean. The spear finds its mark only when the sceptre is straight.

links.quote: that only if it doesn’t bend
brings a ruler victory
It is the sceptre
It is not the spear
links.reason: The spear is named only to be set below the sceptre.

couplets.plain: The ruler guards the whole world. Justice guards him, if he keeps it up without a break.
couplets.pm: The ruler guards all the world, and his own straight sceptre guards him, if he keeps it going even when it meets a block. Think of the ruler who gave justice against his own son, and the one who cut off his own hand.

links.quote: Justice guards him
The ruler guards the whole world

links.remove: The Tamil says justice, not sceptre, so the image isn’t in it.

couplets.plain: A ruler who isn’t easy to reach, and doesn’t look into things and give justice, will sink low and fall by himself.
couplets.pm: A ruler who doesn’t make himself easy to approach for those seeking justice, and doesn’t examine what they say with many learned men and judge by the truth, stands in a low state and perishes by himself. The low state is one of sin and blame. Righteousness is death to wrongdoers, so he falls even with no enemies.

links.quote: isn’t easy to reach
doesn’t look into things and give justice
A ruler who isn’t easy to reach

couplets.plain: To protect his people from others, care for them and punish wrongdoing is no stain on a ruler. It is his work.
couplets.pm: To guard his subjects from others, not to harm them himself, and to punish them when they do wrong is no blame to a ruler, because it is his work. There are three punishments: pain, taking property and death. Here the first two are meant. Punishing those under him may seem unrighteous, but cleansing them of wrong is the duty of his caste.

links.quote: no stain on a ruler
To protect his people from others

couplets.plain: A ruler who punishes the wicked with death is like someone pulling weeds from a green crop.
couplets.pm: A ruler who punishes the wicked with death and protects the worthy is like a farmer who pulls the weeds and saves his green crop. The wicked are arsonists, poisoners, armed killers, thieves, highway robbers, plunderers, adulterers and the like. If he spares them out of pity the world suffers, like a crop among weeds. So killing, too, is the duty of a ruler’s caste.
couplets.sensitive: approves of putting offenders to death

links.quote: pulling weeds from a green crop
A ruler who punishes the wicked with death
links.reason: The Tamil names the ruler as the one who punishes.

ideaLinks.quote: The ruler’s sceptre stands at the root of the books of the sages and of righteousness
ideaLinks.reason: The ruler’s sceptre is named the root of righteousness.
The books of the sages rest on the sceptre and lapse when the ruler fails at justice.

ideaLinks.quote: Rain and harvest come together in the land of a ruler
